slides.0.title: Châteauneuf-du-Pape
slides.0.subtitle: 13 varieties and the galets terroir
slides.1.title: Châteauneuf-du-Pape: the basics
slides.1.highlights.0.title: AOC and date
slides.1.highlights.0.content: Became an AOC in 1936 (Drive notes: 15 May), among France's first; the INAO product page says growers formed their first viticultural union in 1923
slides.1.highlights.1.title: Area
slides.1.highlights.1.content: Five Vaucluse communes — Châteauneuf-du-Pape, Bédarrides, Courthézon, Orange and Sorgues — on the left bank about 15 km north of Avignon
slides.1.highlights.2.title: Size (sources differ)
slides.1.highlights.2.content: INAO text: about 3,200 ha (2010); Drive notes: over 3,000 ha. Inter Rhône's 2025 production table excludes this AOC, so the course says only "around 3,000 ha" and does not test it
slides.1.highlights.3.title: Wines and alcohol
slides.1.highlights.3.content: Dry red and white; yield 35 hl/ha; minimum natural alcohol 12.5%
slides.1.content: Châteauneuf-du-Pape is tied to five Vaucluse communes on the left bank.
slides.2.title: Thirteen varieties (eighteen entries)
slides.2.highlights.0.title: 13 or 18?
slides.2.highlights.0.content: The INAO product page says "a list of 18 varieties with Grenache dominant"; the common "13 varieties" merges colour variants of one variety (Grenache noir, blanc, gris), so the two counts do not conflict
slides.2.highlights.1.title: The 13-variety list (Drive)
slides.2.highlights.1.content: Grenache (noir/blanc/gris), Mourvèdre, Syrah, Cinsault, Counoise, Bourboulenc, Roussanne, Brun Argenté (Vaccarèse), Clairette (incl. Clairette Rosé), Muscardin, Picardan, Piquepoul (noir/blanc/gris) and Terret Noir
slides.2.highlights.2.title: Varieties not on the list
slides.2.highlights.2.content: Marsanne and Viognier are not on the permitted list (CMS materials state that Marsanne may not be used); the specification page shows no minimum Grenache share, only describing Grenache as the dominant variety
slides.2.highlights.3.title: White wine
slides.2.highlights.3.content: The INAO page names Grenache blanc, Clairette and Roussanne among the whites; Drive notes mention Beaucastel's white as Roussanne-led and Rayas's as mostly Grenache blanc (house styles, not tested)
slides.2.content: Every permitted variety may go into red; red and white musts may be blended before fermentation (Drive notes).
slides.3.title: Production rules and le râpé
slides.3.highlights.0.title: Hand harvest and sorting
slides.3.highlights.0.content: The specification requires hand harvesting and bans harvesting machines; quality sorting, in the vineyard or on a table, is mandatory. The growers' document sets bins at 3,000 kg or less
slides.3.highlights.1.title: Other limits (growers' 2021 document; table extraction incomplete, reference only)
slides.3.highlights.1.content: No enrichment, no colour-altering additives, no thermal treatment at or above 40 °C and no agglomerated corks
slides.3.highlights.2.title: Le râpé: percentages differ
slides.3.highlights.2.content: Le râpé is a mechanism for discarding or declassifying part of the crop as a safeguard against underripe fruit. Drive notes say 2%; the growers' 2021 table shows only "AOC lost from 36 hl/ha, or from 42 if râpé is produced". The percentage could not be confirmed in INAO text, so it is flagged and not tested
slides.3.highlights.3.title: The papal-crest bottle (unchecked)
slides.3.highlights.3.content: Many estates use a bottle embossed with the papal crest; the INAO page shows no such rule, so it is a growers' emblem, unchecked and not tested
slides.3.content: Testable: hand harvest, sorting, 35 hl/ha and 12.5%. The le râpé percentage is not tested.
slides.4.title: Terroir and history
slides.4.highlights.0.title: Galets and other soils
slides.4.highlights.0.content: The famous galets roulés cover river terraces, but soils vary far beyond them: gravel, calcareous clay and sandy alluvium (Drive notes)
slides.4.highlights.1.title: The Mistral
slides.4.highlights.1.content: The Mistral brings dryness and sunshine and keeps fruit healthy; the stones store daytime heat and release it at night (common view)
slides.4.highlights.2.title: The papacy and Avignon
slides.4.highlights.2.content: The popes resided in Avignon in the 14th century (1309–1377 per Drive notes), the origin of the "papal new castle" name
slides.4.highlights.3.title: Early estate bottling (single source)
slides.4.highlights.3.content: Drive notes say Château La Nerthe released the first estate-bottled Châteauneuf-du-Pape in 1785; single source, not tested
slides.4.content: Soils, the Mistral and history are the basic vocabulary for describing the style.
slides.5.componentProps.slide.title: 🧠 Knowledge Check
Which of these is NOT on the permitted list for Châteauneuf-du-Pape?
Marsanne is not on the list; Roussanne, Bourboulenc and Picardan are all permitted.
Which of these is a requirement of the Châteauneuf-du-Pape specification?
D. Ageing in new oak is compulsory
Hand harvesting is required and machines are banned; the specification page shows no minimum variety shares, and both red and white are made.
On which bank of the Rhône is Châteauneuf-du-Pape?
On the left bank in Vaucluse; Lirac and Tavel are the right-bank names.
In which year did Châteauneuf-du-Pape become an AOC?
1936. 1923 is when growers formed their union, not the AOC date.
